You then have three choices.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens when points pile up on a New Jersey driving record. The manual sets a clear trigger: a driver who accumulates twelve to fourteen points within a twenty-four-month period receives a Notice of Scheduled Suspension from the MVC by mail. That notice is not the end of the road, because the driver then has choices. You will learn those three choices, who decides the outcome when a driver asks for a hearing, what the Driver Improvement Program takes off the record, who teaches its classes and what they cost, and the one-year probation that follows the program.

lines.text: Twelve to fourteen points.
Within twenty-four months.
The MVC sends a notice by mail.

narration.text: Start with the numbers, because they are easy to mix up with other point rules. The Notice of Scheduled Suspension comes when a driver accumulates twelve to fourteen points within a twenty-four-month period. Both parts matter: the point range and the time window. The MVC sends the notice by mail. Notice the word scheduled. The suspension has been set up, but the notice is followed by choices that the driver can make. Later in this section you will meet other point thresholds, such as the surcharge that starts at six points within three years, so tie this one firmly to twelve to fourteen points in twenty-four months.

lines.text: Attend a Driver Improvement Program.
Ask for a hearing.
Or surrender the license for the suspension period.

narration.text: After the notice arrives, the driver has three choices. First, the driver may attend a New Jersey Driver Improvement Program. Second, the driver may ask for a hearing. Third, the driver may surrender the license for the suspension period. If a driver asks for a hearing and it is granted, someone has to make the call. The manual says the MVC Chief Administrator or an Administrative Law Judge decides whether to suspend driving privileges. So a hearing does not guarantee any result; it hands the decision to one of those two. On a practice question, look for all three choices together: the program, the hearing and surrender.

lines.text: Completion takes three points off.
Taught by approved providers.
Seventy-five dollar MVC fee plus a provider fee.

narration.text: The Driver Improvement Program is the choice that also helps the record. Successfully completing it takes three points off the driver's record. The classes are taught by a licensed Statewide Safety Organization or a New Jersey-licensed driving school approved for that program, and the same is true of Probationary Driver classes. There is a cost to plan for. Before scheduling a Driver Improvement or Probationary Driver class with a private provider, the driver pays the MVC a seventy-five dollar administration fee, plus a separate fee to the provider. So there are two payments, one to the MVC and one to the provider.

lines.text: Finishing the program removes three points.
Then comes a one-year probation.
Any moving violation means a scheduled suspension.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think finishing the Driver Improvement Program wipes the slate clean. It does take three points off, but it also starts a new period to watch. After finishing a Driver Improvement Program, or after having driving privileges restored, a driver serves a one-year probationary period. During that year, any moving violation leads to a scheduled suspension. Not a warning, and not just more points, but a scheduled suspension. So the program is a credit and a commitment together. If a question asks what follows the program, the answer is the one-year probation with that strict rule.

lines.text: Notice received after twelve points.
Driver finishes the program.
What happens next?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver reaches twelve points within twenty-four months, receives the notice, and chooses the Driver Improvement Program. After finishing it, what changes on the record, and what comes next? Work it out before reading on. Successfully completing the program takes three points off the driver's record. Next comes a one-year probationary period, and during that year any moving violation leads to a scheduled suspension. If you also remembered that the driver had two other choices, asking for a hearing or surrendering the license for the suspension period, you have the whole path.

lines.text: Twelve to fourteen points in twenty-four months.
Program, hearing or surrender.
Three points off, then one year of probation.

narration.text: Let us pull this together. Twelve to fourteen points within a twenty-four-month period brings a Notice of Scheduled Suspension from the MVC by mail. The driver may then attend a New Jersey Driver Improvement Program, ask for a hearing, or surrender the license for the suspension period. At a hearing, the MVC Chief Administrator or an Administrative Law Judge decides whether to suspend. The program takes three points off, is taught by a licensed Statewide Safety Organization or an approved driving school, and costs a seventy-five dollar MVC fee plus a provider fee. Then comes one year of probation.

why_how.text: The two-year probationary period begins with a special learner or examination permit, so new drivers are covered from the start.
Two or more moving violations adding up to four or more points require the Probationary Driver Program.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the Probationary Driver Program always removes exactly three points.

correction.text: A finished Probationary Driver Program removes up to three points; exactly three is the Driver Improvement Program credit.

memory_support.text: Permit starts two years; four points sends you to class.

prompt.text: A permit holder has two moving violations adding up to four points. What is required, and what can it earn?

answer.text: Enrollment in the Probationary Driver Program, which can cut up to three points.

rationale.text: Two or more moving violations totaling four or more points during probation require the program, and completing it can cut up to three points.

lines.text: Probation starts with a permit.
Violations can trigger a program.

narration.text: This lesson is about the probationary driver period, which applies to new drivers. A two-year probationary driver period begins once a driver receives a special learner or examination permit. That means the clock starts with the permit itself, not with a later license. In this lesson you will learn what pushes a new driver into the Probationary Driver Program, what completing it earns, what happens if a driver skips it, and how to keep two easy-to-confuse pairs apart: three points versus up to three points, and a one-year probation versus a two-year probation.

lines.text: Two-year period starts with a permit.
Two or more moving violations.
Adding up to four or more points.

narration.text: The trigger for the Probationary Driver Program has two parts, and a question may test either one. During the two-year probationary period, two or more moving violations adding up to four or more points require enrollment in the Probationary Driver Program. So it takes more than one moving violation, and together they must reach at least four points. Remember where the period comes from: it begins once a driver receives a special learner or examination permit. A new driver who is still on a permit is already inside that window. Required is the key word here, because enrollment is not optional once the trigger is met.

lines.text: Completing can cut up to three points.
Skipping it brings a suspension.
Another moving point violation does too.

narration.text: Once enrollment is required, the driver faces a clear fork. Completing the Probationary Driver Program can cut up to three points from the record. That is the reward. The risk side is stated just as plainly: skipping the program, or picking up another moving point violation during the test period, brings a suspension. So finishing the class is not the end of the job either; the driver still has to avoid another moving point violation during that test period. Who teaches these classes? The same providers as Driver Improvement: a licensed Statewide Safety Organization or an approved New Jersey-licensed driving school.

title.text: Exactly three versus up to three

lines.text: Driver Improvement: three points off.
Probationary Driver: up to three off.
Program probation one year; new-driver period two.

narration.text: Here are two traps in one slide. First, the point credits. A finished Driver Improvement Program removes three points, while a finished Probationary Driver Program removes up to three points. The words up to matter, so do not treat them as the same number. Second, the probation lengths. The probation after a Driver Improvement Program or a restoration lasts one year, while the new-driver probationary period that starts with a permit lasts two years. A quick way to sort them: the Driver Improvement track gives exactly three off and one year after; the new-driver track starts at the permit and runs two years.

lines.text: Permit holder, two moving violations.
Four points in total.
What is required, and what can it earn?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver who received a special learner permit picks up two moving violations that add up to four points. What is required, and what can it earn? Work it out before reading on. The driver is inside the two-year probationary period, which began with the permit. Two or more moving violations adding up to four or more points require enrollment in the Probationary Driver Program. Completing it can cut up to three points, not exactly three. And if the driver skips the program, or picks up another moving point violation during the test period, a suspension follows.

lines.text: Probation starts with the permit, for two years.
Two violations totaling four points: program required.
Complete it: up to three points off.

narration.text: To wrap up: a two-year probationary driver period begins once a driver receives a special learner or examination permit. During that period, two or more moving violations adding up to four or more points require enrollment in the Probationary Driver Program. Completing the program can cut up to three points, but skipping it or picking up another moving point violation during the test period brings a suspension. Keep the contrasts straight: a Driver Improvement Program removes three points and is followed by one year of probation, while the Probationary Driver Program removes up to three, and the new-driver period lasts two years.

why_how.text: A voluntary defensive driving course removes two points and may lower the insurance rate, so it helps to know its limit of once every five years.
Each year without a violation or suspension takes up to three points off, but the total never drops below zero.

scenario.text: Morgan finishes a voluntary defensive driving course, then drives a full year without a violation or suspension.

reasoning.text: The course removes two points, and the clean year can take up to three more off the total.

result.text: Morgan's total falls but never drops below zero, and another course will not be credited for five years.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a defensive driving course can be credited every year.

correction.text: The MVC credits a defensive driving course toward point reduction only once every five years.

memory_support.text: Course takes two, clean year takes up to three.

prompt.text: A driver takes a defensive driving course this year and another next year. How much does the first remove, and does the second count?

answer.text: The first removes two points; the second does not count, since the credit is given only once every five years.

rationale.text: A defensive driving course removes two points, and the MVC credits one only once every five years.

lines.text: Courses can remove points.
Clean years lower the total.

narration.text: Points do not only go up. This lesson covers the ways a New Jersey driver can bring a point total down. Finishing a voluntary defensive driving course removes two points from the license and may qualify the driver for a lower insurance rate. There is a limit on how often that credit counts, and there are several ways to take a course, including online options and options for mature drivers. Finally, there is a reduction that needs no class at all: a year of driving without a violation or suspension. You will learn how each one works and how much it takes off.

lines.text: Voluntary course removes two points.
May qualify for a lower insurance rate.
Credited only once every five years.

narration.text: The voluntary defensive driving course has two possible benefits. It removes two points from the license, and it may qualify the driver for a lower insurance rate. Note the word may for insurance; the course may qualify the driver, which is not the same as a guarantee. The point credit has a firm limit: the MVC credits a defensive driving course toward point reduction only once every five years. So a driver cannot take the course every year and keep peeling off two points at a time. If a question offers a yearly course credit, that is a trap; the answer is once every five years.

lines.text: Classroom or approved online providers.
Mature drivers: various schools and organizations.
Six-hour class open to everyone.

narration.text: There is more than one way to take a course. Besides classroom courses, the MVC lists approved online defensive driving providers. Mature drivers aged fifty-five and older can take defensive driving courses at various driving schools or through specific organizations. Various providers also offer a six-hour driver safety class that is open to everyone and also available online. That class can earn a multi-year insurance discount and a two-point reduction where applicable. Notice the matching number: two points, the same credit as the voluntary defensive driving course. The phrase where applicable means the reduction does not fit every case.

title.text: Two points versus up to three

lines.text: Course: two points off.
Clean year: up to three off.
Total never drops below zero.

narration.text: Here is a common mix-up. The defensive driving course removes two points. A clean year is a different tool. Up to three points come off a driver's total for each year without a violation or suspension, but the total never drops below zero. So a driver with no points cannot bank negative points for later. The two tools also differ in what they require: the course is something you finish, and it counts only once every five years, while the clean-year reduction comes from each year you drive without a violation or suspension. When a question says each year, think up to three; when it says course, think two.

lines.text: A course this year.
Another course next year.
How many credits count?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver finishes a voluntary defensive driving course this year and plans to take another one next year to remove more points. How much does the first course take off, and will the second one count toward point reduction? Work it out before reading on. The first course removes two points from the license and may qualify the driver for a lower insurance rate. The second course will not count toward point reduction, because the MVC credits a defensive driving course only once every five years. A year without a violation or suspension, though, can still take up to three points off.

lines.text: Course: two points, once every five years.
Online and mature driver options.
Clean year: up to three, never below zero.

narration.text: To close: a voluntary defensive driving course removes two points and may qualify the driver for a lower insurance rate, but the MVC credits it toward point reduction only once every five years. Besides classroom courses, the MVC lists approved online providers. Mature drivers aged fifty-five and older can take courses at various driving schools or through specific organizations, and a six-hour driver safety class open to everyone can earn a multi-year insurance discount and a two-point reduction where applicable. Each year without a violation or suspension takes up to three points off, and the total never drops below zero.

why_how.text: Six or more points within three years brings a surcharge of one hundred fifty dollars plus twenty-five dollars for each point above six.
Standard point reductions do not apply, and a surcharge is paid every year for three years on top of court fines.

scenario.text: Dana has six points posted within three years and also has a court fine to pay.

reasoning.text: Six points means a one hundred fifty dollar surcharge, paid every year for three years on top of the fine.

result.text: Dana pays both, knowing that unpaid surcharges can lead to collection action such as a lien or wage garnishment.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing a point reduction course will lower a surcharge.

correction.text: Standard point reductions do not apply to the surcharge system.

memory_support.text: Six points, three years, every year you pay.

prompt.text: A driver with six points in three years takes a course that removes two points. What is owed, and does the course help?

answer.text: A one hundred fifty dollar surcharge, paid yearly for three years; the course does not reduce it.

rationale.text: Six points brings the one hundred fifty dollar surcharge, and standard point reductions do not apply to surcharges.

lines.text: Six or more points can bring a surcharge.
Some offenses carry their own.

narration.text: This lesson covers surcharges, which are paid on top of any court fines. They come in two kinds. One kind is based on points: a driver with six or more points within three years owes a surcharge. The other kind is tied to specific offenses, such as driving unlicensed, driving while suspended, having no liability insurance, or a DUI or refusal. You will learn the amounts, when points start to count, why point reductions do not help here, how long the payments last, what happens when surcharges go unpaid, and the penalties a parent or guardian faces for DUI with a passenger under eighteen.

lines.text: Six or more points within three years.
One hundred fifty dollars for six points.
Plus twenty-five dollars per point above six.

narration.text: The point surcharge starts at a clear line. A driver with six or more points within three years owes a surcharge of one hundred fifty dollars for six points, plus twenty-five dollars for each point above six. So the base amount covers the first six points, and every additional point adds twenty-five dollars. Keep this threshold separate from the suspension notice you learned earlier, which comes at twelve to fourteen points within twenty-four months. Six points in three years is about money; twelve to fourteen points in twenty-four months is about a scheduled suspension. Different counts, different windows and different results.

title.text: When points count, and how long

lines.text: Counted from the posting date.
Not the date of the violation.
Keeps applying while six or more remain.

narration.text: Two timing rules shape the point surcharge. First, points count toward surcharges from the date the violation is posted to the record, not the date it happened. So the clock follows the posting date. Second, the surcharge does not stop on its own after one bill. Surcharges apply once a driver has six or more points within three years, and they keep applying for as long as six or more points posted in the preceding three years remain on the record. In other words, the threshold tells you when surcharges start, and the same six-point, three-year test keeps running to decide whether they continue.

title.text: Point credits do not touch surcharges

lines.text: Standard point reductions do not apply.
Paid every year for three years.
On top of any court fines.

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches many drivers. You might think a point reduction, such as a course credit, would shrink a surcharge. It does not. Standard point reductions do not apply to the surcharge system. And a surcharge is not a one-time bill: it is paid every year for three years, on top of any court fines. The fine and the surcharge are separate costs. There is a third cost to keep in mind too. Motor vehicle convictions may also raise the premiums an insurance company charges. So one conviction can mean a court fine, a surcharge each year for three years, and possibly higher insurance premiums.

lines.text: Unlicensed: one hundred dollars a year.
Suspended or uninsured: two hundred fifty a year.
Unpaid surcharges can lead to collection.

narration.text: Some offenses carry their own yearly surcharge. The yearly surcharge is one hundred dollars for driving unlicensed, and two hundred fifty dollars for driving while suspended or for having no liability insurance on a motor vehicle. Notice that driving suspended and driving without liability insurance share the same amount. Ignoring these bills does not make them go away. Unpaid surcharges can lead to collection action, including a Superior Court judgment, a lien on real property or wage garnishment. A question that asks about unpaid surcharges is looking for one of those collection steps, not more points.

title.text: DUI surcharges and a minor aboard

lines.text: DUI or refusal: one thousand dollars a year.
Third offense within three years: one thousand five hundred.
Minor aboard: a disorderly persons offense.

narration.text: The largest surcharges in this lesson belong to DUI. A DUI or refusal carries a one thousand dollar yearly surcharge, which rises to one thousand five hundred dollars for a third offense within three years. Refusal is listed right beside DUI, so it carries the same surcharge. There is a separate rule when a child is in the vehicle. A parent or guardian convicted of DUI with a passenger under eighteen in the vehicle commits a disorderly persons offense, faces up to six months of suspension and must do up to five days of community service. Keep the two facts apart: one is a yearly surcharge, the other is a set of penalties.

lines.text: Six points within three years.
Then a defensive driving course.
Does the surcharge shrink?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver has six points posted within three years and then finishes a defensive driving course that removes two points. What surcharge does the driver owe, and does the course reduce it? Work it out before reading on. Six points within three years means a surcharge of one hundred fifty dollars, the base amount for six points. The course does not help with that, because standard point reductions do not apply to the surcharge system. The surcharge is paid every year for three years, on top of any court fines, and it keeps applying while six or more points posted in the preceding three years remain.

title.text: The cost of points and offenses

lines.text: Six points: one hundred fifty, plus twenty-five each above.
Paid yearly for three years.
DUI: one thousand; third offense, one thousand five hundred.

narration.text: To sum up: six or more points within three years brings a surcharge of one hundred fifty dollars plus twenty-five dollars for each point above six, counted from the date the violation is posted. Point reductions do not apply, and the surcharge is paid every year for three years on top of court fines. Convictions may also raise insurance premiums. Yearly offense surcharges are one hundred dollars for driving unlicensed, two hundred fifty for driving suspended or uninsured, and one thousand for DUI or refusal, rising to one thousand five hundred for a third offense within three years. Unpaid surcharges can lead to collection action.

title.text: Point records, speed and driving manner

why_how.text: Speeding points rise by band, two, four and five, so knowing the bands lets you score any speeding ticket.
Tailgating and reckless driving carry five points while careless driving carries two, which separates the serious manner violations from the lesser one.

scenario.text: Alex is ticketed for speeding fifteen miles per hour over the limit and, weeks later, for careless driving.

reasoning.text: Fifteen to twenty-nine over is the four-point band, and careless driving carries two points.

result.text: Both violations go on Alex's record, and point violations recorded after March one, nineteen seventy-four, stay there permanently.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating thirty miles per hour over the limit as part of the four-point band.

correction.text: Fifteen to twenty-nine over carries four points, but thirty or more over jumps to five.

memory_support.text: Two, four, five as the needle climbs.

prompt.text: One driver speeds thirty over the limit and another drives carelessly. How many points does each get?

answer.text: Five points for thirty over, and two points for careless driving.

rationale.text: Thirty or more over jumps to five points, and careless driving carries two.

lines.text: Each violation has a point value.
Records keep them permanently.

narration.text: This lesson starts the point schedule itself. Every listed violation carries a set number of points, and the record keeps them. Point violations recorded after March one, nineteen seventy-four, stay on a driver's record permanently. You will also learn that traffic laws reach beyond the highway. Then we move into specific values: the three speeding bands, racing on a highway, driving a construction vehicle too fast, and the driving-manner violations, from tailgating and reckless driving to careless and unsafe driving. Many of these numbers sit close together, so we will point out the pairs that are easiest to confuse.

lines.text: Point violations stay on the record permanently.
Laws apply on parking areas and driveways.
Government grounds count too.

narration.text: Two background rules come first. Point violations recorded after March one, nineteen seventy-four, stay on a driver's record permanently. Do not confuse that with your point total. Earlier you learned that up to three points come off the total for each year without a violation or suspension, yet the violations themselves remain recorded. Second, traffic laws apply not only on highways and roadways but also on parking areas, driveways and grounds owned and maintained by government entities. So a careless move in a government parking area is still covered by traffic laws. Think of the record as permanent and the rules as reaching past the main road.

lines.text: One to fourteen over: two points.
Fifteen to twenty-nine over: four points.
Thirty or more over: five points.

narration.text: Speeding points depend on how far over the limit a driver goes. Speeding one to fourteen miles per hour over the limit costs two points. Fifteen to twenty-nine miles per hour over costs four points. Thirty miles per hour or more over costs five points. Notice that the bands skip three: the values run two, four and five. There is also a separate speed rule for a particular kind of vehicle. Driving a construction vehicle faster than forty-five miles per hour carries three points. That rule is about the vehicle and a fixed speed, not about how far over a posted limit the driver goes.

lines.text: Fifteen to twenty-nine over: four.
Thirty or more over: five.
Watch the line at thirty.

narration.text: The two upper speeding bands are the ones most often swapped. Speeding fifteen to twenty-nine miles per hour over the limit carries four points, but thirty miles per hour or more over jumps to five. The line sits exactly at thirty over. Twenty-nine over is still four points; thirty over is five. Five points also matches some other serious violations in this section, such as racing on a highway, which can make five feel like the answer for any fast driving. It is not. Read the number in the question, find its band, and only then choose. Two, four or five, depending on the band.

lines.text: Tailgating and reckless driving: five each.
Racing on a highway: five.
Careless: two; unsafe: four, third or later.

narration.text: Now the manner of driving. Tailgating and reckless driving each carry five points, while careless driving carries two. Racing on a highway also carries five points, and the manual pairs it with failing to yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk at two points. Then comes unsafe driving, which has a special rule. Driving in an unsafe manner carries four points, but only for a third or later violation within five years of the previous one. So careless and unsafe driving are different violations with different point rules: careless is two points, while unsafe brings four points only once it reaches a third or later violation in that window.

lines.text: Speeding thirty over.
Careless driving.
How many points each?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: one driver is ticketed for speeding thirty miles per hour over the limit, and another is ticketed for careless driving. How many points does each violation carry? Work it out before reading on. Speeding thirty miles per hour or more over the limit jumps to five points; fifteen to twenty-nine over would have been four. Careless driving carries two points. If the second driver had instead been convicted of driving in an unsafe manner, four points would apply only for a third or later violation within five years of the previous one. Tailgating or reckless driving would have been five.

lines.text: Records keep point violations permanently.
Speeding: two, four or five.
Tailgating, reckless, racing five; careless two.

narration.text: Here is the summary. Point violations recorded after March one, nineteen seventy-four, stay on the record permanently, and traffic laws also apply on parking areas, driveways and government grounds. Speeding costs two points at one to fourteen over, four points at fifteen to twenty-nine over, and five points at thirty or more over. A construction vehicle driven faster than forty-five miles per hour carries three points. Racing on a highway, tailgating and reckless driving each carry five points, careless driving carries two, and unsafe driving carries four only on a third or later violation within five years of the previous one.

why_how.text: Passing violations cluster at four and five points, so knowing which ones are fives keeps the values straight.
Improper turns and handheld phone use both carry three points, but phone points are assessed only on later convictions.

scenario.text: Sam improperly passes a frozen dessert truck on a local street.

reasoning.text: The manual gives improperly passing a frozen dessert truck four points, while a school bus would be five.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking improperly passing a frozen dessert truck carries the same five points as a school bus.

correction.text: Improperly passing a school bus carries five points, but a frozen dessert truck carries four.

memory_support.text: Bus five, truck four, turns three.

prompt.text: One driver improperly passes a school bus and another a frozen dessert truck. Which costs more points?

answer.text: The school bus, at five points, versus four for the frozen dessert truck.

rationale.text: Improperly passing a school bus carries five points, and a frozen dessert truck carries four.

lines.text: Passing violations carry four or five.
Turns and phones carry three.

narration.text: This lesson covers point values for passing, turning and phone use. Passing violations mostly sit at four or five points, and the difference depends on what was passed and how. Failing to keep to the right of a vehicle coming from the opposite direction carries five points, and several passing mistakes carry four. You will also learn the special point values on the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway and Atlantic City Expressway, the school bus and frozen dessert truck rules, the three points for improper turns, and how points work for using a handheld phone while driving.

lines.text: Not keeping right of oncoming traffic: five.
Passing on the right or off the road: four.
No passing zone: four.

narration.text: Start with the basic passing violations. Failing to keep to the right of a vehicle coming from the opposite direction carries five points. Passing improperly on the right or off the roadway carries four. Improper passing in a no passing zone also carries four points. So among these, the five-point violation is the one involving oncoming traffic, and the passing mistakes carry four. When a question describes a driver who fails to keep right of a vehicle coming the other way, think five points. When it describes passing on the right, passing off the roadway or passing in a no passing zone, think four points.

title.text: Toll roads, buses and dessert trucks

lines.text: Turnpike, Parkway, Expressway: against traffic, two.
Improper passing there: four.
School bus five; frozen dessert truck four.

narration.text: Three named highways have their own listed values. On the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway and Atlantic City Expressway, moving against traffic carries two points and improper passing carries four. Notice that improper passing there matches the four points for a no passing zone. Two kinds of vehicles are named as well. Improperly passing a school bus carries five points, and improperly passing a frozen dessert truck carries four. Both vehicles are named in the manual, but the school bus carries the higher value. If a question asks which of the two costs more, the school bus is the answer at five points.

lines.text: School bus: five; dessert truck: four.
Keep right of oncoming: five.
Passing on the right: four.

narration.text: The trap in this lesson is mixing up the fives and the fours. Here are the fives: failing to keep to the right of a vehicle coming from the opposite direction, and improperly passing a school bus. Here are the fours: passing improperly on the right or off the roadway, improper passing in a no passing zone, improper passing on the three named highways, and improperly passing a frozen dessert truck. A tempting wrong answer gives the frozen dessert truck five points because it sounds like the school bus rule. It is four. And moving against traffic on those three highways is only two points, not four or five.

lines.text: Improper turn at a light: three.
Improper right, left or U-turn: three.
Handheld phone: three, on later convictions.

narration.text: Turns are simpler. An improper turn at a traffic light, an improper right or left turn and an improper U-turn each carry three points. One number covers all of them. Handheld phones also carry three points, but with a twist about when the points are assessed. Using a handheld phone while driving carries three points, assessed on a third conviction within ten years of the second and on every fourth or later offense. So the phone points are tied to repeat convictions, and the timing window is ten years from the second conviction. If a question asks about phone points, look for the third conviction rule.

lines.text: Passed a school bus improperly.
Passed a frozen dessert truck improperly.
Which costs more?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: one driver improperly passes a school bus, and another improperly passes a frozen dessert truck. How many points does each carry, and which costs more? Work it out before reading on. Improperly passing a school bus carries five points, and improperly passing a frozen dessert truck carries four, so the school bus costs more. For comparison, improper passing in a no passing zone is also four points, and failing to keep to the right of a vehicle coming from the opposite direction is five. If you kept the fives and fours apart, you have this lesson's main trap handled.

lines.text: Fives: oncoming traffic, school bus.
Fours: right side, no passing zone, dessert truck.
Threes: improper turns and handheld phones.

narration.text: Let us review. Failing to keep to the right of a vehicle coming from the opposite direction carries five points, and passing improperly on the right or off the roadway carries four. Improper passing in a no passing zone carries four. On the New Jersey Turnpike, Garden State Parkway and Atlantic City Expressway, moving against traffic carries two and improper passing carries four. Improperly passing a school bus carries five, and a frozen dessert truck four. Improper turns each carry three, and a handheld phone carries three on a third conviction within ten years of the second and on every fourth or later offense.

why_how.text: Many common violations carry two points, so grouping them makes the list easier to remember.
Leaving the scene of a crash costs two points when no one is hurt but eight with personal injury.

scenario.text: Robin leaves the scene of a crash in which another driver was injured.

reasoning.text: Personal injury moves the crash scene value from two points to eight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking leaving the scene of a crash always costs two points.

correction.text: It costs two points when no one is hurt, but eight points when there is personal injury.

memory_support.text: No harm two, hurt someone eight.

prompt.text: A driver leaves a crash scene where someone was injured, then fails to yield to an emergency vehicle. How many points each?

answer.text: Eight points for leaving the scene with injury, and two points for not yielding to the emergency vehicle.

rationale.text: Leaving the scene with personal injury costs eight, and failing to yield to an emergency vehicle carries two.

lines.text: Many common violations carry two points.
Leaving a crash scene can carry eight.

narration.text: This lesson gathers many of the two-point violations and then one violation whose value depends on what happened. Failing to obey an officer's direction, failing to observe traffic signals, failing to stop for a traffic light, failing to yield, and failing to obey Stop or Yield signs all appear on the two-point list, along with the Move Over Law. Then we turn to leaving the scene of a crash, which costs two points when no one is hurt and eight points when there is personal injury. Grouping the twos together makes them easier to remember, and the crash scene rule is the contrast to watch.

lines.text: Officer's direction ignored: two.
Traffic signals not observed: two.
Light, flashing red, no signal: two each.

narration.text: Start with directions and signals. Failing to obey an officer's direction and failing to observe traffic signals each carry two points. A closely related group adds more detail. Failing to stop for a traffic light, failing to stop at a flashing red signal and failing to signal properly each carry two points. Notice that this second group mixes stopping for lights with signalling properly, yet every one of them shares the same value. If a question pairs any of these with a point number, two is the value the manual lists for each one. Officer, signals, lights, flashing red and signalling: all two points.

title.text: Yielding and the Move Over Law

lines.text: Not yielding to an emergency vehicle: two.
Not yielding at an intersection: two.
Move Over Law, Stop or Yield signs: two.

narration.text: Yielding violations are also two points. Failing to yield to an emergency vehicle and failing to yield at an intersection each carry two points. Earlier you saw that failing to yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk carries two as well. Next, violating the Move Over Law, failing to obey Stop or Yield signs and committing a moving violation out of state each carry two points. That last item matters for the next lesson, where out-of-state tickets and the interstate compacts come in. For now, file all of these under the two-point list, alongside the officer, signal and traffic light violations from the slide before.

title.text: Leaving the scene: two or eight

lines.text: No one hurt: two points.
Personal injury: eight points.
The injury changes the value.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Leaving the scene of a crash costs two points when no one is hurt, the same as the long list of two-point violations. But when there is personal injury, leaving the scene costs eight points. That is the largest point value in this lesson. A question may describe a crash and simply ask about leaving the scene, so read carefully for whether anyone was hurt. No injury points to two. Personal injury points to eight. Do not settle on two just because it is the most common value on the list, and do not pick five because it sounds serious. The injury is what decides.

lines.text: A crash with an injury.
The driver leaves.
How many points?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver is involved in a crash in which another person is injured, and the driver leaves the scene. Later that week, the same driver fails to yield to an emergency vehicle. How many points does each violation carry? Work it out before reading on. Leaving the scene of a crash with personal injury costs eight points. If no one had been hurt, it would have cost two. Failing to yield to an emergency vehicle carries two points, the same as failing to yield at an intersection. The injury is what raises the crash scene value from two to eight.

lines.text: Officer, signals, lights, yielding: two each.
Move Over Law, Stop or Yield signs: two.
Leaving the scene: two, or eight with injury.

narration.text: To wrap up: failing to obey an officer's direction and failing to observe traffic signals each carry two points. Failing to stop for a traffic light, failing to stop at a flashing red signal and failing to signal properly each carry two. Failing to yield to an emergency vehicle or at an intersection carries two. Violating the Move Over Law, failing to obey Stop or Yield signs and a moving violation out of state each carry two. Leaving the scene of a crash costs two points when no one is hurt, and eight points when there is personal injury. Many violations share two points, but the crash scene with an injury stands apart.

why_how.text: A traffic violation in another state adds two points to a New Jersey record, so out-of-state tickets still count here.
The Nonresident Violator Compact makes visitors satisfy their tickets, while the Driver License Compact shares violation records.

scenario.text: Jordan, a New Jersey driver, gets a moving violation ticket while visiting a member state.

reasoning.text: Jordan must satisfy the citation or risk suspension at home, and the violation becomes part of the New Jersey record.

result.text: The out-of-state violation adds two points to Jordan's New Jersey record.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a ticket from another state never affects a New Jersey record.

correction.text: Under the Driver License Compact, violations from other member states become part of the New Jersey record, and an out-of-state violation adds two points.

memory_support.text: Answer it there, it lands here.

prompt.text: A New Jersey driver is ticketed in a member state. What must the driver do, and what happens to the home record?

answer.text: Satisfy the citation or risk suspension, and the violation joins the New Jersey record.

rationale.text: The Nonresident Violator Compact requires satisfying the citation, and the Driver License Compact puts the violation on the home record.

lines.text: Out-of-state violations still count.
Two compacts link the states.

narration.text: This lesson follows a ticket across state lines. A traffic violation committed in another state adds two points to a New Jersey record, so driving elsewhere does not keep a violation off your record here. Two interstate agreements explain how that works. The Nonresident Violator Compact deals with drivers who get a ticket while visiting a member state. The Driver License Compact deals with sharing violation records between member states. You will learn what each one does, which places and violations the Nonresident Violator Compact covers and excludes, the protections nonresident drivers keep, and how to tell the two compacts apart.

lines.text: Violation in another state: two points.
Out-of-state moving violation: two points.
It lands on the New Jersey record.

narration.text: Start with the points. A traffic violation committed in another state adds two points to a New Jersey record. The point list says the same thing in a different way: committing a moving violation out of state carries two points. That point value is the same as many in-state violations, such as violating the Move Over Law. How does a ticket from another state reach New Jersey at all? That is the job of the Driver License Compact. Under it, violations from other member states become part of a driver's New Jersey record. So the record travels with you, and the out-of-state violation shows up with two points.

lines.text: Ticketed in a member state? Satisfy the citation.
Otherwise, risk suspension at home.
Answer for tickets as residents would.

narration.text: The Nonresident Violator Compact covers what happens when a visiting driver gets a ticket. Under it, a driver ticketed in a member state must satisfy the citation or risk suspension in their home state. Put another way, the compact makes visiting drivers answer for tickets as residents would. A driver cannot simply drive home and forget about a ticket from another member state, because the citation still has to be satisfied or suspension at home is the risk. So the key words for this compact are visiting driver, satisfy the citation, and risk of suspension at home. Those words separate it from the other compact.

lines.text: Forty-four states plus the District of Columbia.
Excludes parking or standing, weight limit, hazmat.
Due process kept; no detention.

narration.text: The Nonresident Violator Compact has a defined reach. It covers forty-four states plus the District of Columbia. It also has exclusions: it does not cover parking or standing violations, weight limit violations or hazmat violations. So a question about a parking ticket under this compact should lead you to the exclusion. The compact also protects drivers. Nonresident drivers keep due process protection and cannot be detained out of state under that compact. That is the balance it strikes: visiting drivers must satisfy their citations, but they keep due process and are not held in the other state while that happens.

lines.text: Nonresident Violator: answer the ticket.
Driver License: share the record.
Do not swap them.

narration.text: Here is the trap: the two compact names sound alike, and answer choices may swap their jobs. The Nonresident Violator Compact makes visiting drivers answer for tickets as residents would. The Driver License Compact shares violation records so out-of-state tickets land on the home record. A memory aid is in the names. Nonresident Violator is about the violator who is not a resident, the visiting driver who must satisfy the ticket. Driver License is about the license record, where violations from other member states become part of the New Jersey record. If an answer choice describes record sharing, it belongs to the Driver License Compact.

lines.text: A New Jersey driver ticketed elsewhere.
In a member state.
What happens at home?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a New Jersey driver gets a moving violation ticket while visiting a member state. What must the driver do about the ticket, and what happens to the New Jersey record? Work it out before reading on. Under the Nonresident Violator Compact, the driver must satisfy the citation or risk suspension at home, and the driver keeps due process protection and cannot be detained out of state. Under the Driver License Compact, the violation becomes part of the New Jersey record, and a traffic violation committed in another state adds two points to that record. One compact handles the ticket; the other handles the record.

lines.text: Out-of-state violation: two points.
Nonresident Violator: satisfy the citation.
Driver License: violations join the record.

narration.text: To close this lesson: a traffic violation committed in another state adds two points to a New Jersey record. Under the Nonresident Violator Compact, a driver ticketed in a member state must satisfy the citation or risk suspension in their home state. It covers forty-four states plus the District of Columbia and excludes parking or standing, weight limit and hazmat violations, and nonresident drivers keep due process protection and cannot be detained out of state. Under the Driver License Compact, violations from other member states become part of the New Jersey record. One compact makes you answer the ticket; the other shares the record.
